tagline: A forest loop links paper towns, river crossings and mountain views.
intro: The Woodland Heritage Trail makes a 65-mile loop through northern New Hampshire, circling the Kilkenny District of the White Mountain National Forest. Its NH 110 stretch winds through mountainous country; elsewhere the journey follows the Androscoggin River and passes pull-offs with views of the Presidential Range. New Hampshire’s tourism office presents the route as a celebration of the region’s wood-products heritage.

One piece of the corridor’s road history begins in 1826, when Thomas, Amos and Daniel Green built a road from Berlin to Gorham. Falls on the Androscoggin powered sawmills, and by 1885 Berlin had several pulp and paper mills. The mills’ demand for workers brought immigrants from Russia, Norway, Finland and other countries, as well as French Canadians from Quebec. In Groveton, Wausau stopped paper production in 2008, ending that mill’s role in the region’s industry.

Beginning at Lancaster, follow US 3 north to Groveton, then NH 110 east through Stark, where the covered bridge crosses the Upper Ammonoosuc. Continue toward Milan by NH 110A and NH 110B, then take NH 16 south beside the Androscoggin past the Nansen Ski Jump to Berlin and Gorham. US 2 returns west through Randolph and Jefferson to Lancaster, with King Ravine on Mount Adams visible near Randolph.

moments.title: Stark Covered Bridge
moments.text: Stark’s white covered bridge carries a road across the Upper Ammonoosuc, linking Northside Road with NH 110. Its central support has changed more than once. A flood carried away the bridge and its original granite pier; the bridge survived and was put back on its abutments. Laminated arches were added, but sagging later prompted a temporary wooden pier. Rebuilding in 1954 replaced those arches with a concrete pier and steel stringers. The concrete support flares upstream to deflect debris, while pendant acorn finials decorate the white bridge. Before the covered bridge was built, a floating bridge crossed the river a short distance upstream.

moments.title: Nansen Ski Jump
moments.text: The Nansen Ski Jump rises beside Route 16 in Milan, just north of Berlin. Berlin and the National Youth Administration built it in 1936, with a steel frame 175.3 feet high. Olympic trials followed in 1938. The jump closed in 1988 and fell into disrepair. Brush clearing began in 2015; decking repairs in 2016 and 2017 prepared it for Olympian Sarah Hendrickson’s celebratory jump on March 4, 2017. It is now part of the Nansen Ski Jump State Historic Site. Its name commemorates Fridtjof Nansen, the Norwegian explorer and humanitarian, and the state owns and manages the jumping facility.

moments.title: Randolph
moments.text: Near Randolph, the road has views into King Ravine, a glacial cirque on Mount Adams. US 2 divides the northern slopes of the Presidential Range from the mountains on the town’s north side. The woods also have a history of repair: the Randolph Mountain Club began in 1910 to restore trails damaged by logging. Travel changed here, too. Vacationers once reached hotels by horse-drawn carriage from the train station. As automobiles became more popular, hotels declined and private vacation homes became more common. The club operates four camps in the White Mountain National Forest: two enclosed cabins and two partially enclosed shelters.
